name: Hollow Cairn
geological_features: Heavily cratered surface with no evidence of geological renewal
A large impact basin dominating the southern hemisphere
Regolith layers meters deep composed of pulverized rock and glass beads
specific_features: Anomalous low-density readings suggesting extensive subsurface void spaces
A perfectly circular depression of unknown origin on the equatorial plain
description: Hollow Cairn is a dead world in every sense, a battered sphere of grey rock and dust that has not known geological activity in billions of years. Its surface is a palimpsest of impact craters layered over one another in overlapping rings, the regolith ground to a fine powder that clings to everything and holds the sharp-edged footprints of survey boots with perfect fidelity. The southern hemisphere is dominated by a massive impact basin that stripped away the original crust and exposed the darker mantle rock beneath.

Without atmosphere, the sky above Hollow Cairn is pure black even at local noon, the stars unwavering points of light above a landscape of absolute stillness. The temperature differential between sun-facing and shadow-facing slopes is brutal, a hundred-degree swing across a single ridgeline that fractures exposed rock faces with audible pops as thermal stress exceeds material tolerance. Nothing moves here that is not pushed by an impact or pulled by the faint gravity.

The most puzzling feature of Hollow Cairn is what lies beneath its surface. Density measurements consistently return values lower than the body's composition should produce, suggesting extensive void spaces in the interior. A perfectly circular depression on the equatorial plain, too geometrically regular to be a natural crater, has fueled speculation ranging from collapsed lava tubes to artificial excavation, though no evidence supports the latter hypothesis. Two subsurface survey missions have been proposed and neither has been funded.

Hollow Cairn's practical value is modest: accessible iron and silicon in quantities sufficient for local construction needs but not worth long-haul extraction. Its real draw is the mystery of its interior voids and the circular equatorial anomaly. Fringe theorists claim it as evidence of ancient alien mining operations, while geologists insist on more mundane explanations involving impact-generated fracture networks. Until someone drills deep enough to settle the question, Hollow Cairn will continue to sit at the intersection of science and speculation, quietly accumulating dust.
